Distraught

dih-STRAWT -- from Latin distrahere, 'to pull apart': a distraught mind feels pulled in every direction. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Distraught is deeply upset and agitated.

The distraught owner papered the whole neighborhood with flyers for her missing cat.

Worked Example

Hours after the ferry docks and every passenger walks off, a mother whose son isn't among them paces the terminal, phone shaking in her hand, unable to finish a sentence.

That state of being nearly pulled apart by worry and grief is exactly what distraught describes. Unlike 'sad,' which can be quiet and calm, distraught means agitated to the point of losing composure.

Antonyms

How Strong Is It? — upset → distraught → frantic

upset vs. distraught

upset vs. distraught: Upset is far milder than distraught -- you can be upset about a bad grade and still function, while distraught means so shaken that composure is gone.

frantic vs. distraught

frantic vs. distraught: Frantic adds wild motion to what distraught describes: a distraught person is overwhelmed by distress, while a frantic one is racing around in a desperate whirl of activity.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — dis-

prefix — dis-: apart (Latin)

root — -traught

root — -traught: to pull, draw (Latin (trahere))

Put it together

Put it together: Distraught grew out of Latin distrahere, 'to pull apart' -- dis- ('apart') plus trahere ('to pull') -- a distraught person feels pulled to pieces by emotion, the same root that gives us distract and tractor.

Use the root in a new word: distract

Use the root in a new word: distract: The circling fly kept trying to distract her during the chess final.

Root Check

Word Choice

Distraught usually pairs with 'over' or 'at' -- 'distraught over the loss,' 'distraught at the news' -- and describes visible, agitated distress, stronger than upset and tied to a specific shock.
